summary.text: A 45-year-old woman with hypertension treated with atenolol, previously independent in daily activities, presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of chest pain, dry cough, nocturnal fever, nausea and malaise. On admission she was febrile, tachycardic and tachypneic with bilateral pulmonary crackles, and had leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein and diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest radiography; CURB-65 was 2 and the Pneumonia Severity Index was Class IV.

Testing for viral and atypical pathogens was negative. She was started on amoxicillin/clavulanate plus azithromycin and admitted to the ICU, developed worsening tachypnea and hypoxemia, and required oxygen and non-invasive ventilation, then orotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation. Blood and sputum cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae with bacteremia; antimicrobials were escalated to piperacillin-tazobactam and later ceftazidime plus linezolid.

On day 6 of ICU stay a chest CT showed extensive bilateral parenchymal necrosis with multiple cavitated lesions, establishing necrotizing pneumonia. She progressed to severe ARDS refractory to protective ventilation and prone positioning and on day 7 was transferred to a tertiary center for VV-ECMO, which lasted 29 days; tracheostomy was performed on day 11 of that stay.

She spent 38 days in the tertiary center ICU and was then returned to the referring hospital for 10 additional days, for a total hospital stay of 55 days. She survived and was discharged home with residual muscular weakness.

summary.text: A 39-year-old woman, previously independent, with a history of heterozygous Factor V Leiden mutation and recurrent deep-vein thrombosis on chronic apixaban presented with a five-day history of pleuritic back pain, dry cough and progressive dyspnea. On arrival she was acutely ill, hypotensive, tachycardic, tachypneic and hypoxemic with severe type 1 respiratory failure and elevated lactate; CURB-65 was 3 and PSI 144 (Class IV).

Chest radiography showed bilateral infiltrates and CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism, with bilateral ground-glass opacities, small consolidations and pleural effusions. Viral and atypical testing was negative. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was started; she was admitted to the ICU, intubated, ventilated and given vasopressor support. Blood and sputum cultures grew MSSA, prompting escalation to intravenous flucloxacillin.

Despite targeted therapy she developed worsening respiratory failure and multiorgan dysfunction including acute kidney injury (AKIN 2), hepatic impairment and coagulopathy. On day 6 of hospitalization a repeat chest CT showed extensive bilateral parenchymal necrosis with cavitated nodules and abscesses, establishing necrotizing pneumonia, with a small left pleural empyema and a right bronchopleural fistula.

Oxygenation kept declining despite a trial of prone positioning, and she was transferred to a tertiary cardiothoracic center for VV-ECMO consideration. She improved without ECMO, and the fistula needed no surgery after surgical evaluation. After 15 days in the tertiary ICU and 12 days back at the referring hospital (33 days total) she survived and was discharged home with residual muscular weakness and anxiety.

summary.text: A 61-year-old previously autonomous man with long-term smoking (36 pack-years), hypertension, dyslipidemia, peripheral arterial disease, hepatic steatosis and chronic daily alcohol consumption presented with a five-day history of productive cough, progressive dyspnea and three days of fever. On arrival he was febrile, tachycardic, hypotensive and tachypneic with type 1 respiratory failure and hyperlactatemia; CURB-65 was 3 and PSI 143 (Class IV).

Laboratory evaluation showed leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, AKIN stage 2 kidney injury and raised urea and CRP. Admission radiograph and CT showed bilateral infiltrates, ground-glass opacities and consolidation, and viral and atypical testing was negative. He received high-flow nasal oxygen, ceftriaxone and azithromycin; blood cultures grew Streptococcus pneumoniae and penicillin G was added, and he was admitted to the ICU.

Over the following days he developed progressive multiorgan dysfunction with AKIN stage 3 kidney injury, and antimicrobials were escalated to meropenem plus linezolid from days 10 to 11. A repeat chest CT confirmed necrotizing pneumonia with marked radiological progression from admission. On day 11 he developed severe anuria, rapidly rising creatine kinase and refractory metabolic acidosis, and CRRT with an HA380 hemoadsorption cartridge was started.

Acidosis persisted and organ failure progressed despite CRRT. Because of worsening hypoxemia, escalating norepinephrine requirements and severe multiorgan dysfunction he was deemed ineligible for ECMO rescue, evolved to refractory shock and died later the same day, after a hospital stay of 11 days.
